premises.text: Seniors face walker-related falls from forgotten brakes and steep ramps, with high injury costs and lasting fear
premises.evidence_span: steep ramps and forgetfulness is what causes walk-related fall injuries

premises.text: A smart walker uses pressure sensors, encoders, and accelerometers to perceive intention and environment and actuate brakes
premises.evidence_span: capable of perceiving user intention, the environment around us, and actuating appropriately to minimize the risk of injuries

premises.text: Sitting automatically engages brakes; descending ramps applies gradual braking for stability
premises.evidence_span: when a senior sits on the walker, automatically brakes kicks in and prevents a fall from happening

premises.text: Go-to-market is licensing the technology to walker manufacturers for factory integration
premises.evidence_span: license it to walker manufacturers. They integrate it into their walkers as they leave the factory

value.text: Seniors avoid walker-related falls and keep a higher quality of life
value.evidence_span: safeguard seniors from falls, leading them to a higher quality of life

secondary_value.evidence_span: help seniors reduce fall-related injuries, alleviate healthcare expenses

causal_links.evidence_span: walk-related fall injuries, it can cost on average of $17,500
apply gradual brakes, slowing them down, giving them that immediate support and stability

notes: Forgetfulness and steep-ramp pains folded as one fall-risk bundle in P1. Sensor array and sit/ramp brake behaviors treated as one smart-walker mechanism with P3 detailing the two actuation modes of that mechanism (could be seen as cascade; kept P3 as the concrete safety behaviors claimed). Baby-boom market sizing left as framing. Singletons D1 and D3 retained as separately revisable problem and licensing modules. Anti-template: need/product/channel justified by distinct revisability of fall problem, device mechanism, and OEM license path.
